name: The Lakeshore Corridor
description:
The Lakeshore Corridor is not a place. It is the connective tissue between places -- the artery that links every settlement on the eastern Lake Michigan coast from the Indiana border to the Mackinac Straits. In the old world it was two highways: Interstate 196 running from the Indiana line to Grand Rapids, and US Route 31 continuing north to the Straits. In 2200 they have been merged, expanded, and redesignated as GLMZ Regional Corridor 31 -- a hybrid transit route carrying automated cargo convoys, civilian vehicles, maglev-adjacent freight pods, and the constant low-grade traffic of a coastline that moves things for a living.

The Corridor is the most dangerous and most essential piece of infrastructure on the eastern shore. Dangerous because it passes through or adjacent to every jurisdiction on the coast -- Ringo security zones, Axiom cargo territories, Helix sovereign land, Verdana agricultural zones -- and each transition point is a border where the rules change and the enforcement doesn't always announce itself. A vehicle that is legal in one stretch may be flagged three kilometers later. A cargo load that passes Axiom inspection at the Mill may be seized by Verdana agricultural quarantine near the Tulip Protocol. The Corridor is a legal patchwork, and the people who drive it professionally have memorized the transitions the way sailors memorize reefs.

The rest stops and service nodes along the Corridor have developed into their own micro-economies. Every forty to sixty kilometers, a cluster of fuel stations, repair shops, food vendors, and informal markets has grown up around the official rest infrastructure. These nodes are where the Corridor's gray economy operates -- cargo is reclassified, manifests are adjusted, passengers change vehicles, information is traded. The nodes operate in the jurisdictional gaps between corporate territories, which makes them ungoverned in the technical sense and self-governed in the practical sense. Each node has its own character, its own regulars, its own rules. Collectively they form a network that parallels the official Corridor infrastructure -- a shadow highway running alongside the real one, carrying the commerce that the official economy pretends doesn't exist.

Driving the Corridor at night is a specific experience. The lake is visible in glimpses between the industrial and agricultural zones -- dark water catching starlight or the reflected glow of distant cargo platforms. The automated convoys run nose-to-tail in the freight lanes, their navigation lights forming a ribbon of motion that stretches to the horizon in both directions. The service nodes glow in the darkness like embers. And between the nodes, between the zones, there are stretches of the old road where the infrastructure thins and the forest closes in and you could be driving the same highway in 1980 or 2200, because some roads don't change even when everything around them does.

sights: Automated cargo convoys in the freight lanes -- hundreds of vehicles moving in synchronized formation, navigation lights blinking in patterns that communicate to each other, not to humans
Jurisdictional transition markers -- holographic boundary projections that change color and language as you enter each corporate zone
Service nodes glowing at irregular intervals along the route, each one a distinct cluster of light and activity
Lake Michigan glimpsed between zones -- dark water, cargo platform lights on the horizon, the occasional flash of a Ringo patrol vessel
The old road surface visible in patches where the automated lane infrastructure hasn't been extended -- cracked asphalt from the 20th century, stubborn and historical
sounds: Tire noise and wind -- the constant soundtrack of highway travel, unchanged by a century of technology
Automated convoy communication -- data bursts that sound like rhythmic clicking if you're on the right frequency
Service node activity as you approach -- engines, music, the hum of commerce
Jurisdictional alerts from your vehicle's navigation system, announcing each zone transition with corporate-branded audio
Silence between nodes -- the specific quiet of a highway at night between populated areas
smells: Road -- asphalt, rubber, the universal smell of long-distance driving
Lake air blowing inland, carrying different chemical signatures depending on which stretch of coast you're passing
Service node food -- the Corridor's rest stops have developed competitive cuisine, and the debate about which node has the best smoked fish is older than some of the buildings
Agricultural zones -- Verdana's engineered orchards produce a sweet, pharmaceutical smell that drifts across the highway during pollination season
atmosphere.feel: The Corridor feels like circulation. You are inside the bloodstream of the eastern shore, moving with or against the flow of goods, people, and information that keeps the coast alive. There is a freedom to highway travel that even corporate jurisdiction cannot fully contain -- the feeling of being between places, belonging to none of them, accountable only to the road and the distance. This is why the Corridor's gray economy works. In transit, you are nobody's citizen. You are just moving.

demographics: No permanent population on the Corridor itself. Service node populations range from 200 to 2,000 each, predominantly Tier 1-2 with the specific demographics of highway communities: transient, practical, suspicious of authority, and hospitable to strangers who follow the rules. Approximately 40,000 vehicles use the Corridor daily, carrying an estimated 200,000 people.
economy: Official Corridor toll revenue: Φ890 million annually. Automated cargo convoy fees: Φ3.2 billion. Service node economies: estimated Φ400 million combined, of which roughly half is gray market. The Corridor's informal economy is essentially a distributed marketplace operating in the jurisdictional gaps -- goods, services, information, and identities all change hands at the nodes.
power_structure: The GLMZ Transit Authority nominally administers the Corridor, but actual authority fragments across every corporate zone it passes through. Each service node has its own informal power structure -- typically a long-term operator or family that controls the fuel supply and therefore controls everything else. A loose network of Corridor regulars -- truckers, couriers, gray-market runners -- maintains an informal code that keeps the nodes functional and the violence to levels that don't invite corporate crackdowns.
dangers: Jurisdictional transitions -- crossing a zone boundary with the wrong cargo, credentials, or vehicle modifications can result in seizure, detention, or worse
Automated convoy proximity -- the freight lanes are not designed for human drivers, and the convoys do not stop for obstacles
Service node disputes -- the informal code works until it doesn't, and disagreements between node operators can strand travelers in dangerous locations
Isolation between nodes -- breakdowns on empty stretches of the Corridor can be life-threatening, especially in winter
Corporate security patrols -- each zone monitors its section of the Corridor, and some are more aggressive about non-standard traffic than others
opportunities: The gray market economy is distributed and resilient -- reliable runners with clean records can move anything between the coast's settlements
Information gathered across multiple service nodes creates a picture of coast-wide traffic patterns that has intelligence value
The jurisdictional gaps are the Corridor's greatest asset -- understanding which gaps exist where is expertise worth paying for
Service node businesses are always looking for reliable supply, security, and technical support
story_hooks: A new service node is being established in a jurisdictional gap between Axiom and Ringo territories, and both corponations want to control it without officially acknowledging it exists

Automated cargo convoys have been arriving at their destinations with manifests that don't match their contents -- and the discrepancies are occurring on stretches of Corridor where no human hands touch the cargo

A Corridor regular -- a long-haul runner who has driven the route for thirty years -- has noticed that the distance between two service nodes has changed, which should be impossible, and yet her odometer doesn't lie

adjacent_to: Every coastal settlement between them (lateral connections at each node)
GLMZ (western connection via multiple feeder routes)

frequented_by: Long-haul cargo operators running coast-length routes
Gray-market runners moving goods between the jurisdictional gaps
Service node operators and their communities
Corporate security patrols monitoring their respective zones
